title: The Bernstein–Vazirani Algorithm
summary: Find a whole secret string with one query.
objectives: Recover a hidden n-bit string s with one query to the oracle
Read s from the final register state, taking the qubit ordering into account
Explain why a randomized classical algorithm still needs n queries
mission: Find the hidden 4-bit string s with a single call to oracle(qc): at the end, the input register (qubits 0 to 3) must be in |s⟩. Qubit 0 is the last character of s, so s = s3 s2 s1 s0 and the state label is |q3 q2 q1 q0⟩.

prediction.question: A randomized classical algorithm may err with probability 1%. Can it find a 4-bit secret string with fewer than 4 queries?
prediction.explanation: Each query returns one bit. With fewer than 4 queries, several strings remain consistent with the answers, and the best guess is correct with probability at most 1/2, far from 99%. Randomization does not help. The quantum algorithm uses one query for any length of s.

hints: The circuit is the Deutsch–Jozsa circuit with 4 input qubits and the auxiliary qubit on qubit 4.
Prepare the auxiliary qubit in |−⟩ with qc.x(4) and qc.h(4). Apply Hadamards to qubits 0 to 3 before and after the oracle.
Use for qubit in range(4): qc.h(qubit), once before and once after oracle(qc).

challenge.mission: Solve Bernstein–Vazirani with 4 qubits and no auxiliary qubit. The hidden oracle is now a phase oracle, phase_oracle(qc), which maps |x⟩ to (−1)^(s·x ⊕ b)|x⟩ on qubits 0 to 3 (the bias b only contributes a global phase). Call it once in a circuit qc with 4 qubits so that the register ends in |s⟩, with qubit 0 as the last character of s. The function oracle(qc) is not available.
hints: The phase oracle already writes the phase (−1)^(s·x), so the auxiliary qubit in |−⟩ is not needed.
Hadamard on every qubit, phase_oracle(qc), Hadamard on every qubit.
qc = QuantumCircuit(4); for q in range(4): qc.h(q); phase_oracle(qc); for q in range(4): qc.h(q).
